paragraphs.text: Lesson 22. Ethical marketing.
Mitch and Brent are business partners who work in advertising.
They are debating whether to take on a particular project.
Listen and answer the comprehension questions.
We've got to think of a clever slogan.
If this client likes her stuff, we'll be rolling in dough.
Whoa, hold your horses.
Let's take it one step at a time.
You know I've been having second thoughts about whether we should even take on this job.
What? Come on Brent.
This is the top supplement company in the world.
It's our chance to break into the big leagues.
But the product in question is kind of dubious.
A very controversial new energy drink that hasn't been approved by the Food and Drug Administration.
I'm not sure I can market that in good conscience.
These energy drinks are all arranged nowadays.
If we come up with a killer advertisement targeted towards teens, these drinks will be flying off the shelves.
Yeah, it's just that this product is still in a trial stage.
If anything goes wrong, it could be a catastrophe for the company.
And for us too.
But once the FDA okay's it, then sure we can go for it.
You want to wait for the FDA?
Don't hold your breath.
They take forever to approve a product.
And by the time they do, our client will have found a new advertising team.
We will have missed the boat.
Missing the boat is better than being smacked with a lawsuit of people start getting sick from this energy drink.
I'm not about to risk my neck for 10 pounds of sugar, caffeine and who knows what else crammed into a tiny bottle.
What are the odds of us getting sued though?
People will go after the manufacturer, not the advertiser.
You're being too cautious.
And you're being too reckless.
Not only could we end up losing money on lawsuits, but we'd also lose our reputation.
And that's not easy to recover from.
What if we take on the client, but tone down the messaging of the ads?
And of course we'd have a disclaimer that the energy drink isn't FDA approved.
I don't know. I've just got a gut feeling that this one's a bad bet.
Plus we've got no shortage of clients.
Let's make our millions with a product we can actually be proud of.
Okay. If you're not sold on this project, then we'll have to turn it down.
It'd be too much for me to take on solo.
So much for our big break.
I'm sure another great opportunity will come along.
And look on the bright side. At least we'll be able to sleep better at night.
Okay. Let's learn the vocabulary.
Mitch wants to think of a clever slogan for the campaign.
A slogan is a short, memorable phrase that's used in advertising.
Mitch says, if this client likes our stuff, we'll be rolling in dough.
Rolling in dough is a slang way to say, having a lot of money.
But Brent says, whoa, hold your horses.
Hold your horses is an informal way to say, wait.
Don't be so quick to take action.
Brent admits that he's been having second thoughts about whether they should even take on the job.
Having second thoughts means reconsidering or doubting a previous decision.
Mitch is stunned at Brent's hesitation.
He says that this is their chance to break into the big leagues.
The big leagues means a high level of activity or competition.
But Brent says that the product in question is kind of dubious.
Dubious means questionable or subject to doubts.
And Brent's not sure that he can market it in good conscience.
In good conscience means without feeling guilty.
Mitch argues that energy drinks are all the rage nowadays.
All the rage means extremely popular.
And Mitch adds, if we come up with the killer advertisement, these drinks will be flying off the shelves.
The phrasal verb, come up with, means to create or invent.
And a killer advertisement.
Killer is a slang way to say, excellent or very effective.
The result would be that the drinks will be flying off the shelves.
Flying off the shelves means selling very fast.
But Brent says that if anything goes wrong, it could be a catastrophe for the company and for us.
A catastrophe is a very big disaster.
However, once the FDA okayes the product, then they can go ahead.
Okayes is an informal way to say approves.
The word okay is actually being used as a verb here.
Mitch replies, you want to wait for the FDA?
Don't hold your breath.
Don't hold your breath means don't wait for it because it will never happen.
Mitch thinks that by the time they get approval, they will have missed the boat.
Missed the boat means missed the opportunity.
Brent's response is that missing the boat is better than being smacked with a lawsuit.
Being smacked with a lawsuit means getting hit with legal action against you, if people start getting sick from the energy drink.
He says, I'm not about to risk my neck.
To risk your neck means to take a risk that could result in a very serious disaster.
Brent describes the energy drink as 10 pounds of sugar, caffeine and who knows what else crammed into a tiny bottle.
Crammed means put into a small space.
Mitch asks, what are the odds of us getting sued though?
What are the odds is another way to say what are the chances?
And he accuses Brent of being too cautious.
Brent accuses Mitch of being too reckless.
Reckless means irresponsible, acting without being careful.
Mitch proposes an idea.
We could tone down the messaging of the ads.
To tone down means to make something less intense or less shocking.
But Brent has a gut feeling that this one's a bad bet.
If you've got a gut feeling, it means you have a feeling of certainty that is deep and hard to explain rationally.
You just know it deep inside you.
He's got a gut feeling that this one's a bad bet.
A bad bet is a potential project that is likely to have bad results or bad consequences.
And Brent points out, we've got no shortage of clients.
No shortage of clients means no lack of clients.
In other words, they have a lot of other clients.
Mitch finally gives in.
He says, if you're not sold on this project, then we'll have to turn it down.
Not sold on means not convinced of the value of.
And the project would be too much work for Mitch to take on solo.
Solo is another way to say alone.
Mitch then says, so much for our big break.
So much for means this is the end of or this will not happen.
And a big break is a fortunate moment when you become famous or successful.
So Mitch is saying that they will lose the moment or the opportunity to become famous or successful.
Brent tries to cheer him up by saying I'm sure another great opportunity will come along
and look on the bright side, at least we'll be able to sleep better at night.
Look on the bright side means consider the positive aspects.
And sleep better at night means to be calm and not feel anxious or agitated.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
